data.body:
Read **Same Digits, Different Values — Decimals** with a partner or use read-aloud. Explore **Key Words**, then play Matching and Memory. Use **Keep the Ideas Clear** as a reference. Try **Sort and Explain**, **Explain Your Thinking**, and **Check Your Understanding**. Use **Remember the Ideas** to build a memory cue. Read **Questions to Explore**, then complete **Try It with Evidence**.

Explain an answer using a detail from the lesson. Pictures support the original activities. Exact diagrams and classroom cartoons have different roles.

Picture panels: Parts of the same whole; Compare and rename; Check a representation; Explain with evidence. Exact grids represent amounts; cartoons provide context only and are not scale drawings. In the sorting pictures, all ten small hundred-grids together form one whole of 1,000 equal cells. Enlarge images to inspect single cells. Colored cells are read left to right within each small grid, then through the top row of grids before the bottom row.

history.title: Same Digits, Different Values — Decimals
history.data:
## Same Digits, Different Values

Two ribbons measure 0.6 meter and 0.45 meter. Which is longer? The number 45 is greater than 6, but that does not settle this question. We must compare the same units.

A **decimal** uses place value to show whole amounts and parts of one. Each **digit** has a value based on its place. The **point** separates the ones place from the tenths place. It is a marker, not a command to ignore units.

Split one meter into ten equal parts. Each part is a **tenth**. Split a tenth into ten equal parts. Each smaller part is a **hundredth**. Split a hundredth into ten equal parts. Each new part is a **thousandth**. Moving one place right makes the unit one tenth as large.

The ribbon that is 0.6 meter long is six tenths of a meter. We can also name it as sixty hundredths: 0.60 meter. Now compare 60 hundredths with 45 hundredths. The first ribbon is longer.

**Equivalent** decimals name the same value. Adding a zero at the right end of a decimal's fractional part does not change its value. For example, 2.5 and 2.500 are equal. But inserting a zero between other digits can change the value. The numbers 2.05 and 2.5 are not equal.

To **compare** two decimals, start with the greatest place and work right. Compare ones, then tenths, then hundredths, as needed. The first unequal place decides which number is greater. With 3.407 and 3.47, the ones and tenths match. Write 3.47 as 3.470. Zero hundredths are fewer than seven hundredths, so 3.407 is less.

A **unit** tells what an amount measures. Use the same unit and the same whole in a drawing. Six tenths of a small ribbon need not be longer than half of a much larger ribbon. A model is useful only when we know what counts as one.

Explain your answer with a place-value name, an equivalent decimal, or a carefully scaled model. Counting written digits is not a comparison rule.

questions.question: Explain why 0.52 is greater than 0.507.
questions.expectedAnswer: Write 0.52 as 0.520. The tenths match, but two hundredths exceed zero hundredths, so 0.520 is greater than 0.507.

questions.question: Why does 4.20 equal 4.2 while 4.02 does not?
questions.expectedAnswer: Twenty hundredths equal two tenths. In 4.02 there are zero tenths and two hundredths, so it is a different value.

data.question: Does a longer decimal always have greater value?
data.answer: No. The values of its places matter. For example, 0.9 is greater than 0.125.

data.question: Can I add a zero anywhere?
data.answer: No. A zero at the far right of the fractional part preserves value. Inserting one elsewhere may change the places.

data.question: Is 0.500 three times as much as 0.5?
data.answer: No. Both name one half. More written digits do not multiply the amount.

data.question: Why keep the same whole in a model?
data.answer: The parts get their size from the whole. Comparing different wholes can hide which numerical value is greater.
